title: Why measurements of water in olivine disagreed, and how to calibrate them
text: This post walks through Towbin, Plank, Klein and Hauri (2023), Measuring H2O Concentrations in Olivine by Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry: Challenges and Paths Forward, published in American Mineralogist. The two sets of standards that most labs use to calibrate water measurements in olivine disagree by about 50%. We traced the offset to their reference values and proposed a calibration that avoids it.

title: Why measurements of water in olivine disagreed, and how to calibrate them
text:
The measurement problem
Olivine, the most common mineral in the upper mantle, holds only tens of parts per million of water. That small amount still matters: it changes how easily the mantle flows and melts, and how much water the planet stores at depth.
Measuring it is hard. The two common methods, FTIR spectroscopy and secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS), are both relative. Each needs calibration against standards whose water content was measured some other way. For olivine, almost every lab relies on one of two standard sets: the olivines of Bell et al. (2003), whose water was measured by nuclear reaction analysis, and those of Withers et al. (2012), measured by elastic recoil detection. FTIR calibrations based on the two sets disagree by about 40%, and it was not clear why.

title: Why measurements of water in olivine disagreed, and how to calibrate them
text:
What we did
We measured olivines from both standard sets in the same SIMS session, so the instrument conditions were identical, and compared each set against its own reference values.
The two sets fall on calibration lines with very different slopes. The Withers et al. line has about half the slope of the Bell et al. line, so the same SIMS signal reads as roughly twice as much water if you calibrate with the Bell et al. olivines. That offset of about 50% is close to the 40% already seen in FTIR. The Bell et al. olivines were also less reproducible: repeat measurements of the same crystal varied by more than 40%, which fits earlier reports that some of them contain tiny hydrous inclusions.



SIMS calibration lines from one session. The Bell et al. olivines (light green circles, water measured by nuclear reaction analysis) define a line about twice as steep as the Withers et al. olivines (blue hexagons, measured by elastic recoil detection). Repeat analyses of KLV23 spread widely along the x-axis at a single reference value. The orthopyroxene standards (dark green) fall between the two, and the dashed line is the orthopyroxene calibration after we revised its reference values. Shaded bands are 95% confidence intervals from bootstrap resampling; the inset (b) shows the full concentration range. Figure 2 from Towbin et al. (2023), American Mineralogist.


An offset like this could come from the reference values or from the two sets of olivines absorbing infrared light differently. The SIMS signal does not depend on how the hydrogen is bonded in the crystal, while infrared absorption can. So we plotted infrared absorbance against the SIMS signal for the same olivines, which leaves the reference values out entirely. Once the infrared spectra exclude the bands from hydrous inclusions, both sets fall on one line. That puts the disagreement in the reference water contents, the nuclear reaction and elastic recoil analyses.



Infrared absorbance against the SIMS signal for the same olivines. The Withers et al. olivines (blue diamonds) and the natural olivines including the Bell et al. samples (pink pentagons) fall on nearly the same line once the infrared spectra exclude the bands from hydrous inclusions. The small orange pentagons are the Bell et al. samples with those bands included. Figure 3 from Towbin et al. (2023), American Mineralogist.

title: Why measurements of water in olivine disagreed, and how to calibrate them
section: Fitting lines when both axes are uncertain
text:
Fitting lines when both axes are uncertain
Calibration data have uncertainty on both axes: the SIMS signal and the reference concentration. Ordinary least squares assumes all the error is in y, which biases the slope. I fit the calibration lines with orthogonal distance regression and estimated their uncertainty by bootstrap resampling; those are the lines and shaded bands in the calibration figure above. I later cleaned up that code and released it as a Python package, odr_bootstrap.

title: Why measurements of water in olivine disagreed, and how to calibrate them
text:
Recommendations

The Withers et al. olivines gave the tightest calibration line, but very little of that material exists.
Orthopyroxene standards make a practical substitute for SIMS: their calibration slope is similar to olivine’s. After we revised their reference values, the orthopyroxene line falls within 12% of the Withers olivine line, inside the long-term uncertainty of the measurements.
With that calibration, the partition coefficient for water between olivine and melt comes out at 0.0009 ± 0.0003. That brings experiments and natural melt-inclusion studies into closer agreement.




Olivine-melt partition coefficients for water. (a) Published values from experiments (circles) sit well above those from melt inclusions (triangles). (b) Recalculated with the orthopyroxene-based calibration, the experimental values move down toward the melt-inclusion values, averaging 0.0009 (blue band). Figure 5 from Towbin et al. (2023), American Mineralogist.


Figures reproduced from Towbin, Plank, Klein and Hauri (2023), American Mineralogist, published by the Mineralogical Society of America.

title: PyIRoGlass: fitting infrared baselines with PCA and Bayesian sampling
text: PyIRoGlass is an open-source Python package that measures water and carbon dioxide in volcanic glass from infrared spectra, with uncertainties. Our paper describing it is in Volcanica, and this post explains the idea behind it.

title: PyIRoGlass: fitting infrared baselines with PCA and Bayesian sampling
text:
Drawing the baseline
Volcanologists measure water and CO₂ in tiny pockets of glass trapped inside crystals (melt inclusions) to work out how deep magma was stored and how much gas it carried. Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy is the most common way to do it. Each dissolved species absorbs at its own wavenumber, and the height of its peak gives the concentration.
The hard part is the baseline. The carbonate peaks that record CO₂ sit on a curved background next to a water peak, and the shape of that background changes from sample to sample. For decades most people drew the baseline by hand. That is slow, it differs between analysts, and it gives no uncertainty on the result.

title: PyIRoGlass: fitting infrared baselines with PCA and Bayesian sampling
text:
Learning what baselines look like
Instead of guessing the baseline for each spectrum, we learned it from data. We collected spectra of melt inclusions from the Aleutians and of back-arc basin glasses with no detectable CO₂. Some of them still had a water peak at 1635 cm⁻¹, so we first described the shape of that peak with its own principal component analysis (PCA) and subtracted it, leaving spectra that are baseline only. PCA on that set gives a mean baseline plus a few components that describe how real baselines vary.



Principal components of the baseline. Each panel shows the mean baseline (black) plus and minus one component. A small number of components covers the range of baselines seen in real glasses. Figure 3 from Shi et al. (2024), Volcanica, CC BY 4.0.


Each new spectrum is then fit as a combination of those baseline components plus the peaks. A Bayesian sampler (Markov chain Monte Carlo) explores all the combinations that fit the data, so every concentration comes with an uncertainty instead of a single number.



A full PyIRoGlass fit for one melt inclusion. (A) The whole spectrum. (B–D) Water peaks in the near- and mid-infrared. (E) The best-fit baseline (dashed), the fitted water and carbonate peaks, and the sampled baselines that set the uncertainty. (F) The residual between the fit and the measured spectrum. Figure 9 from Shi et al. (2024), Volcanica, CC BY 4.0.

title: PyIRoGlass: fitting infrared baselines with PCA and Bayesian sampling
text:
Results
PyIRoGlass results agree with independent analyses of experimentally devolatilized glasses within 6%, and with interlaboratory standards within 10% for water and 6% for CO₂. The paper also updates the molar absorptivities (the constants that convert peak height to concentration) for basaltic glasses, with their uncertainties. The code is open source and on GitHub.
The project began with my idea of learning the baseline shape with PCA, and I did the first PCA analysis. Daniel Rasmussen provided most of the spectra, and Sarah Shi, the lead author, carried the project forward and built PyIRoGlass into the finished tool.
Figures reproduced from Shi, Towbin, Plank, Barth, Rasmussen, Moussallam, Lee and Menke (2024), Volcanica 7(2), 471–501, under a CC BY 4.0 license.

title: Olivine Phenocryst
text:
These images were produced using X-ray computed tomography to demonstrate the three dimensional structure and inclusions of volcanic crystals the size of sand grains. Volcanologists use these crystals to study magma movement prior to eruptions. The crystals and magma glass trapped inside them, known as melt inclusions, offer windows into the magma’s chemical history. The crystal’s chemistry teaches us about the temperature of the magma when it grew. Changes to that chemistry can record the mixing of magmas in the volcano’s plumbing system and give estimates of time between mixing during eruptive run-up and the eruption. Additionally, we can measure volatiles (H2O, CO2, S, F, Cl) trapped inside these inclusions to learn about the gases driving the eruption. Diffusive loss of these volatiles from melt embayments and the crystal itself record ascent rates as magmas move up through the volcanic plumbing system.
X-ray computed tomography data was collected at the American Museum of Natural History’s Microscopy and Imaging Facility and processed in collaboration with scientists at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory and the University of Nevada, Reno.

title: Studying the Winston Red diamond at the Smithsonian
text: The Winston Red is a 2.33-carat red diamond that went on display at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History in April 2025. A team from the Smithsonian and the Gemological Institute of America (GIA) studied it before the unveiling, and our paper is in Gems & Gemology: A Study of the Winston Red: The Smithsonian’s New Fancy Red Diamond.

title: Studying the Winston Red diamond at the Smithsonian
text:
A very rare stone
Red is the rarest diamond color. Of more than a million colored diamonds GIA has examined, about 0.07% were red, and only about two dozen unmodified Fancy red diamonds over one carat are known. The Winston Red is the fifth-largest known Fancy red. It has an old-style cut, and its history goes back at least to 1938, when Cartier sold it to the Maharaja of Nawanagar. Ronald Winston later acquired it and donated it to the Smithsonian in 2023.

title: Studying the Winston Red diamond at the Smithsonian
text:
A lab in a museum
We packed a truck with spectrometers and microscopes at GIA’s lab in Manhattan, drove it to Washington, and set up a temporary lab at the Smithsonian to study the diamond there.



The pavilion of the Winston Red under the microscope. (A) A chip between pavilion facet P1 and the culet. (B) The pavilion facets, labeled P1 to P8 from the chip. (C) Graining seen through facet P2. Photomicrographs by W. Henry Towbin, Figure 7 in Farfan et al. (2025), Gems & Gemology.

title: Studying the Winston Red diamond at the Smithsonian
text:
Where the red comes from
The red is linked to deformation. Deep in the earth the crystal was squeezed hard enough to slip along planes in its structure, leaving fine bands of color (“graining”) in three directions, spaced about 9 to 33 micrometers apart. Under crossed polarizers the graining shows up clearly, along with a “Rose channel,” a hollow tube that forms where two sets of deformation twins cross.



Graining in three directions on one facet, in true color (left) and in black and white to bring out small changes in hue (right). The three directions are marked a, b and c. Images by W. Henry Towbin, Figure 8 in Farfan et al. (2025), Gems & Gemology.


Cathodoluminescence images show the dislocations arranged in a cellular network, a pattern typical of deformed diamonds with little nitrogen. The color itself comes from an absorption band near 550 nm, the band that makes pink and red diamonds pink and red. It is associated with deformation, but its atomic structure is still unknown. In the Winston Red that band is strong enough, and balanced well enough with the nitrogen-related absorptions, to produce a pure red.
The infrared spectra show about 83 ppm nitrogen, mostly in its most aggregated form, and no “platelets,” a defect that heating or strong deformation can destroy.

title: Studying the Winston Red diamond at the Smithsonian
text:
Where it came from
The stone’s origin is not recorded, so we compared its nitrogen content and aggregation state with those of 399 Fancy red diamonds measured by FTIR at GIA. Those measurements and its color pattern place it in Group 1, the pink and red diamonds that formed in Proterozoic cratons, continental cores 0.5 to 2.5 billion years old. That rules out the sources of the other group, such as South Africa, Russia, Tanzania and Canada. Argyle in Australia, the largest source of Group 1 reds, was not discovered until 1979, four decades after Cartier sold the stone, and no red diamonds have been reported from India. The most likely sources left are the river deposits of Venezuela and Brazil, which were producing diamonds before 1938.
Images from Farfan et al. (2025), Gems & Gemology 61(1), © GIA.

title: Making reference glasses for measuring volcanic gases
text: Our paper on the ND70 reference glasses came out in Geostandards and Geoanalytical Research: Moussallam, Towbin, Plank et al. (2024). It describes a set of basaltic glasses with known amounts of water, CO₂, sulfur, chlorine and fluorine, made so that labs can calibrate their instruments over the full range found in nature.

title: Making reference glasses for measuring volcanic gases
section: A gap in the calibration data
text:
A gap in the calibration data
Much of what we know about volcanic gases comes from tiny glass inclusions trapped in crystals, measured with an ion probe (SIMS). SIMS is a relative method: it only gives concentrations if you calibrate it against glasses whose composition is already known.
The available basaltic standards did not cover the range of real samples. Water calibrations above about 1 wt% were extrapolated, and the CO₂ standards stopped near a few hundred ppm, well below many natural melts. Any measurement outside that range depended on a straight line drawn past the last data point.

title: Making reference glasses for measuring volcanic gases
text:
Making the glasses
The ND70 series was made to fill that gap. We started from a single basalt, added known amounts of water, CO₂, sulfur, chlorine and fluorine, and melted each mix at 1 to 1.5 GPa in a piston-cylinder press so the gases stayed dissolved. The series spans 0 to 6 wt% water, 0 to 1.6 wt% CO₂, and 0 to 1 wt% sulfur, chlorine and fluorine. Older standards from earlier studies were included so the labs could cross-check them against the new ones.
Labs in the US, France and Japan then measured the glasses by several independent methods: elastic recoil detection, nuclear reaction analysis, an elemental analyzer, infrared spectroscopy, electron microprobe, and SIMS at four different ion-probe facilities.



Measured water content against the amount loaded into each glass, for seven different methods and labs. Points fall close to the 1:1 line. Figure 1 from Moussallam et al. (2024), Geostandards and Geoanalytical Research.

title: Making reference glasses for measuring volcanic gases
text:
What we found
The amounts we loaded and the amounts measured agree well across methods and labs, so the glasses can serve as reference materials.
We also found a problem with how SIMS measures carbon. The more water a glass contains, the weaker its carbon signal. Measuring a glass with 4 wt% water against standards with less than 2 wt% water could underestimate its CO₂ two- to three-fold, and the reverse mismatch overestimates it. The fix is to calibrate with standards whose water content matches the samples, which the ND70 series now makes possible.



The SIMS carbon signal per unit of CO₂ falls as the water content of the glass rises, in every session and at every lab. Figure 8 from Moussallam et al. (2024), Geostandards and Geoanalytical Research.

title: Making reference glasses for measuring volcanic gases
text:
Where the glasses are now
Pieces of each glass went to ion-probe labs in the US, Europe and Japan. The rest are held at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, where any researcher can borrow them.
I helped start the project after finding gaps in the basaltic glass standards available for calibrating water and CO₂ by SIMS and FTIR. I ran the piston-cylinder experiments at Lamont-Doherty and helped coordinate the analyses across the labs.
Figures reproduced unchanged from Moussallam et al. (2024), Geostandards and Geoanalytical Research 48(3), 637–660, under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

title: Mantle rocks start melting on their way to the surface
text: Our paper on melting in mantle xenoliths is out in the Journal of Petrology: Towbin and Plank (2026), Decompression Melting of Peridotite Xenoliths.

title: Mantle rocks start melting on their way to the surface
section: Rocks from the mantle, delivered by volcanoes
text:
Rocks from the mantle, delivered by volcanoes
Xenoliths are pieces of the Earth’s mantle that a rising magma rips off and carries to the surface. They are one of the few direct samples we have of rock from tens of kilometers down, so geologists use them to work out what the mantle is made of and how it behaves.
Many xenoliths contain thin veins of glass and small crystals, the remains of a little melt. The question is when that melt formed. If it formed deep in the mantle, it records something about the mantle. If it formed during the trip up, it records the trip, and anyone reading the rock as a purely mantle sample needs to know that.



The path the xenoliths took. They sat in the mantle at about 40 km depth and a little over 900 °C until the magma picked them up and heated them to its own temperature, near 1300 °C (black arrow). They then rose with the magma (purple arrow). Most of that path lies above the peridotite solidus (dashed green line), so the xenoliths could start to melt on the way up. Figure 1 from Towbin and Plank (2026), Journal of Petrology.

title: Mantle rocks start melting on their way to the surface
text:
What we measured
We studied xenoliths and the basalt that carried them from a small cinder cone north of the Grand Canyon (Sullivan Ranch, Arizona).
First I scanned whole xenoliths with micro-CT, a 3D X-ray method, and segmented the scans to find the melt veins. The veins run through every xenolith we looked at, connect to each other at the millimeter scale, and make up about 10% of the rock. Many contain gas bubbles.



Inside the melt veins. (a) A slice through a micro-CT scan of a xenolith, with melt veins outlined in yellow; the black spots are bubbles. (b) to (d) Electron images and an element map of the crystals and glass inside a vein. Figure 3 from Towbin and Plank (2026), Journal of Petrology.


Then I measured the minerals and glass with the electron microprobe, the SEM and laser-ablation mass spectrometry. From those analyses we worked out what the melt was (a basalt) and which minerals melted to make it. The reaction is close to what laboratory melting experiments produce at about 1 GPa, a little shallower than where the xenoliths started.



Melt veins in two xenoliths. (a) Optical scan of a thick section, with the veins in yellow, found by thresholding the image. (b) False-color element map of a second xenolith: melt veins yellow, olivine green, orthopyroxene brown, clinopyroxene turquoise, spinel pink. Veins cover about 10% of the area in both. Figure 2 from Towbin and Plank (2026), Journal of Petrology.

title: Mantle rocks start melting on their way to the surface
text:
A clock in the olivine
Olivine crystals next to the veins are zoned: their iron and magnesium contents change from the edge of the crystal inward. That zoning comes from atoms diffusing after the melt appeared, and diffusion runs at a known rate for a given temperature. Fitting a diffusion model to each profile tells you how long the crystal sat next to the melt.



Fitting diffusion models to olivine profiles. Left: electron images with the measured traverse (orange arrow). Right: measured forsterite content (grey points), the assumed starting profile (dashed) and the best-fit diffusion model (solid). Top: olivine next to a melt vein, about 21 days. Middle: olivine at the edge of the xenolith in contact with the carrying magma, about 8.5 days. Bottom: a loose olivine crystal in the lava, about 2.5 days. Figure 14 from Towbin and Plank (2026), Journal of Petrology.


The olivine next to the melt veins gave one to three weeks. Olivine on the outside of the xenoliths, which exchanged with the carrying magma, gives a similar timescale of about a week. So the melting inside the rock happened during the same few weeks the xenolith spent in the magma, not long before in the mantle.
The outer olivine also times the trip itself: 3 to 10 days from pickup to eruption. Over the 40 km the xenoliths travelled, that is an average ascent rate of 0.05 to 0.15 meters per second, similar to rates estimated for other cinder-cone eruptions.

title: Mantle rocks start melting on their way to the surface
text:
Why it matters
In the mantle these rocks were too cool to melt. Once the magma picked them up, it heated them to its own temperature, and the rise did the rest: as the pressure drops, the temperature at which peridotite starts to melt drops too, so a rock that is already hot can begin to melt without getting any hotter. Because the carrying magma is hot and the trip takes days to weeks, we think this kind of melting is hard to avoid in xenoliths brought up by similar volcanoes.
Melting consumes clinopyroxene, so a xenolith that started as one rock type (lherzolite) can end up looking like a more depleted one (harzburgite). The carrying magma also seeped into the outer centimeter or so of each xenolith. Studies that use xenoliths to describe the mantle should check for both effects, and avoid the outer centimeter when they can.



What happens on the trip up. The magma picks up the xenolith, the xenolith heats and starts to melt, and olivine begins exchanging iron and magnesium with both the melt veins and the magma. Growing gas bubbles push magma into the outer edge of the xenolith. After eruption the vein melt loses water, cools and crystallizes. Figure 16 from Towbin and Plank (2026), Journal of Petrology.

title: Mantle rocks start melting on their way to the surface
text:
The tools
The diffusion modeling used a 1-D numerical model I wrote in Python, with kriging to interpolate the measured profiles. The code is on GitHub, and the data are in the paper’s supplement and the EarthChem Library.
This paper started as the second chapter of my PhD at Columbia, with Terry Plank.

title: Henry Towbin
text:
I’m a scientist in Brooklyn, NY. I use Python to analyze scientific data, combining my own measurements (spectroscopy, micro-CT, electron microprobe and SIMS) with published datasets and physical models to answer research questions.
Most recently I was a postdoctoral fellow at the Gemological Institute of America (2023 to 2025), where I built data pipelines for FTIR and Raman spectra of diamonds. Before that I did my PhD at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory on how mantle rocks change on their way to the surface, and before graduate school I ran micro-CT and electron microscopy at the American Museum of Natural History.
I’m looking for data science roles in New York City and am also open to imaging and geoscience work. The posts below cover my research and code; my software is on GitHub.
